name: RF-Mem

paper.title: Evoking User Memory: Personalizing LLM via Recollection-Familiarity Adaptive Retrieval

construction.unit: raw chunk: one user query + one assistant reply (PersonaMem) or one session (PersonaBench, LongMemEval)
construction.processing: none; chunks are embedded as they are

organization.stores: one FAISS inner-product index per user history
organization.index: sentence-embedding vectors (multi-qa-MiniLM-L6-cos-v1 in the main runs; MPNet and BGE also tested)

retrieval.query: question embedding; in recollection rounds, the query is mixed with cluster centroids (α-mix plus the original query)
retrieval.candidates: probe top-10 by cosine; the mean score and softmax entropy decide between one-shot top-K (familiarity) and iterative retrieve-cluster-mix (recollection)
retrieval.selection: familiarity: top-K; recollection: KMeans into B clusters per round, keep B best branches, collect new chunks until K
retrieval.budget: K = 10 chunks on PersonaMem (≈3.6k tokens at 32K)

use.context: retrieved raw chunks joined before the question, instruction and options

classify.note: A retrieval-only method over an unchanged embedding index; the gate and the recollection loop are fixed rules on similarity scores, with no LLM or reranker.

stages.ingestion: User history is cut into chunks: a user query plus the assistant reply for PersonaMem, one session for PersonaBench and LongMemEval.
stages.organization: Chunks are embedded with a sentence encoder into one flat inner-product index; nothing is summarized, linked or updated.
stages.retrieval: A top-10 probe gives a mean cosine and a softmax entropy; a high mean or low entropy takes the one-shot top-K path, otherwise a recollection loop retrieves (B+r)·F chunks, clusters them with KMeans, mixes each centroid into the query and searches again until K new chunks are gathered.
stages.answer: The retrieved raw chunks are placed before the question, a fixed multiple-choice instruction and the options, and the LLM picks one option.

summary: A retriever-only memory method: a probe's mean score and entropy route each question either to plain top-K search or to an embedding-space loop that clusters hits and mixes centroids into the query, with no LLM in retrieval.
notes: Venue: ICLR 2026 poster (OpenReview f7p0F2X6XN, venue 'ICLR 2026 Poster'); arXiv comment 'Accepted by ICLR 2026'. Code checked at d6a2cb3416e8320bcb1439921d319729aeccec8e (2026-02-25, latest commit). The released repo has per-dataset scripts; the PersonaMem path (personamem_data/) is taken as the reference for the generation results. sources.code_note: Latest commit d6a2cb34 (2026-02-25), after the ICLR camera-ready. Scripts sweep α and τ rather than fixing them. As released, personamem_data/main_batch.py reads cmd_args.rag, which the argument parser never defines, and LongMemEval/run.sh calls a file named RF_emem.py that does not exist, so the scripts need small fixes to run. Data files are stored with Git LFS.

headline: Nothing is written or rewritten: memory is the raw dialogue, cut into chunks and embedded. The method is only the retriever.
The gate and the recollection loop use embeddings only (cosine, entropy, KMeans, vector mixing); no LLM or reranker runs before the answer.
Baselines are the same index read other ways (dense top-K, recollection always on, full context, no memory); no other memory system is compared.

open_questions: α and τ are swept in the scripts and the chosen values are not reported, so it is unclear whether the RF-Mem rows use settings picked on the test questions.
PersonaBench and LongMemEval report only recall of sessions, not answer accuracy, so the retrieval gains there are not shown to change answers.
Under MiniLM, 203 of 263 PersonaBench questions (77%) go to recollection, so the gate mostly selects the slow path there.

One flat vector index per user is the whole memory; nothing is summarized, linked or updated.

text: A top-10 probe measures how familiar the question is from the mean cosine and the entropy of the scores; familiar questions get plain top-10 search.
Otherwise hits are clustered, each centroid is mixed into the query, and the search repeats until 10 new chunks are found.

discussion.takeaway: Deciding per question whether to do a plain top-K search or a few embedding-space expansion rounds gives small but consistent gains over always doing either, at near dense-retrieval latency.

claims.claim: Best overall accuracy at every corpus size with compact inputs.
claims.evidence: PersonaMem 0.6350 / 0.5394 / 0.4589 at 32K / 128K / 1M vs dense 0.5908 / 0.5259 / 0.4518; full context 0.6129 at 32K with 24.7k tokens vs 3.6k. Table 1

claims.claim: Gating is cheaper than always recollecting and at least as accurate.
Familiarity suits fact lookups, recollection suits context-heavy questions.
claims.evidence: PersonaBench Pref-Hard Recall@10 0.6267 (recollection) vs 0.5561 (familiarity) under MiniLM. Table 2, §3.3
RF-Mem matches or beats both modes in overall Recall@5/10 on PersonaBench and LongMemEval-S/M for MiniLM, MPNet and BGE. Tables 2-3

claims.claim: Works as a layer over other memory designs.
claims.evidence: Best overall with a MemoryBank summary index (0.5314), HyDE expansion (Recall@10 0.5194) and Search-o1 (0.6146). Tables 4-6

limits: Evaluated only on text dialogue memory.
List entropy and similarity scores are rough proxies for task difficulty and semantic ambiguity.
The index is static: no temporal updates or conflicts across sessions are modeled.
Better surfacing of old history may expose sensitive information.
reading: Gains over dense retrieval shrink with corpus size: +0.044 at 32K, +0.0135 at 128K, +0.0071 at 1M overall accuracy (Table 1).
The code's entropy is the paper's H divided by K (mean instead of sum), and its recollection output is the first 10 chunks collected rather than the top 10 by score.
App. B lists all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as a PersonaBench encoder while Tables 2, 17 name all-mpnet-base-v2; §3.2 gives 7.12 ms for 1M recollection while Table 1 says 8.12 ms.
The released PersonaMem script calls gpt-4.1-mini, which the paper never names; α and τ are swept in the scripts and the reported choice is not stated.
Only the question is embedded, with no LLM query rewriting, so the comparison is against dense top-K on the same index rather than against other memory systems.

abstract.text: RF-Mem borrows the recollection-familiarity idea from memory research to decide how hard a personalized LLM should search its user history. A quick probe search yields a mean similarity and an entropy over the scores; if the question looks familiar the system returns the top-K chunks at once, and otherwise it runs a few rounds that cluster the hits, blend each cluster centroid into the query and search again. Everything happens in embedding space over raw dialogue chunks, with no LLM in the loop. On PersonaMem, PersonaBench and LongMemEval the authors report higher accuracy or recall than plain dense retrieval and full-context prompting at close to one-shot latency.
